> 觀。盥而不薦，有孚顒若。

The twentieth hexagram is the pair to the nineteenth, and its character has already cost this book two corrections.

## 觀 is 從見，雚聲

說文: 觀，諦視也。從見，雚聲.

A phonetic compound. 見 is the semantic side, 雚 the sound.

雚 is an owl — sharp-eyed — so the sound carries a suggestion of seeing accurately. That is 聲中有義, sound with sense inside it, and it is still not a picture.

Which is the third instance of the same error in this series: 訟 (從言公聲), 謙 (從言兼聲), now 觀. The pattern is worth naming: when a phonetic compound happens to have meaningful components, commentary starts reading it as 會意, and the reading it produces is always smoother than the truth.

## Two directions in one character

觀 in the 易 carries two senses: looking outward at things, and looking inward at oneself.

The whole hexagram is built on that split, and the lines distribute it: the first two look out badly, the middle two look out properly, the last three look back in.

## 盥而不薦

盥 is washing the hands — the purity at the start of a sacrifice. 薦 is presenting the offerings.

So: the reverence of the washing, without the ceremony of the offerings.

有孚顒若 — 顒 is grave, solemn, still.

The sentence describes a moment before anything has been presented: the trust is already visible, and the full rite has not begun.

Which is the hexagram's definition of what makes an impression. Not the performance. The state before the performance, which the audience can see and cannot be shown.

## 童觀 / 窺觀

Line 1: 童觀 — the looking of a child, near and shallow. 小人無咎，君子吝: no fault for a small person, blocked for a noble one. The failure is not the shallow sight; it is shallow sight in someone whose charge requires more.

Line 2: 窺觀. 說文 窺，小視也 — peering through a gap. 利女貞.

Note what the text does not do: it does not condemn the narrow view. It assigns it. A view through a crack is correct for the position that has only a crack.

## 觀我生 / 觀其生

Line 3 and line 5 both say 觀我生; line 6 says 觀其生.

生 here is life, vital condition, one's own conduct and state. 觀我生 is turning the look back on oneself, and line 3 uses it to decide advance or retreat.

(An alternative reading takes 生 as 生民, the people one has generated, which the 象 supports at line 5. This book keeps both and says which it is using.)

Line 6: 觀其生 — looking at others' condition, and correcting oneself by it.

So the upper half of the hexagram is a ladder of reflection: self (3), the realm's light (4), self as ruler (5), others as mirror (6).

## 觀國之光，利用賓于王

Line 4: to see the light of the realm, and to be fit to be a guest of the king.

The best line of the hexagram is about being received, and its condition is that one has actually looked at the place one is entering.

## 省方，神道設教

The 象: 省方 — inspect the four quarters, observe the customs, and set instruction according to what the people actually are.

And 神道設教, which is routinely read as superstition and is the opposite. 天道 is soundless and formless; the four seasons run without error — that is what 神道 means. The sage copies that: not compulsion by severity, but the unspoken effect of a settled order.

設教 is therefore not the invention of a doctrine. It is the arrangement of conditions in which people are affected without being told.

## The test

Take a judgement you formed recently about something outside you. Ask whether it was 童觀, 窺觀, or 觀國之光 — and then ask the question the upper half insists on: what did it show you about your own condition. The hexagram's structure says the second question is not optional.
